title: Predict, Optimize, Deliver: Demand Forecasting and Resource Optimization for a Market Research Firm
authors: Mariano, M. T. G.; Monreal, R. N.
venue: The 9th International Conference on Business and Information Management (ICBIM 2025)
tldr: Developed an integrated Predict-Then-Optimize framework combining time-series forecasting (ARIMA, Holt-Winters, Prophet, LSTM) with Pyomo-based resource allocation to address demand uncertainty and workforce optimization in a market research firm.
problem_and_motivation: Professional service firms face highly variable client demand and rely on human resources as their primary asset, but manual workforce planning fails to adapt to demand volatility. Existing forecasting-optimization frameworks are typically designed for product-based or static planning contexts and lack relevance for the time-sensitive, high-variance nature of professional services.
approach: Historical time-tracking data from January 2018 to December 2024 was filtered to billable entries and aggregated daily.
Four forecasting models—ARIMA, Holt-Winters Exponential Smoothing, Prophet, and LSTM—were implemented in Python and tuned via grid search across multiple train-test splits (60:40, 70:30, 80:20).
Model evaluation used RMSE, MAE, and MAPE on a 30-day holdout set, with a weighted error score and additional interpretability/speed penalties for practical deployment.

Selected Prophet forecasts were operationalized as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) problem in Pyomo, solved with CPLEX to allocate six employees across two clients under work-hour caps and availability constraints.
The optimization model was tested under baseline, over-forecasting, and under-forecasting scenarios using RMSE-derived forecast bands.
The framework was deployed within an interactive Power BI dashboard for real-time operational visualization.
findings: num: Prophet achieved the lowest weighted error for Client 1 (13.038) and strong results for Client 2 (27.786), outperforming ARIMA, Holt-Winters, and LSTM.
num: Prophet's overall weighted score (10.456) ranked first when interpretability and speed were factored in, compared to ARIMA (11.582), LSTM (11.634), and Holt-Winters (13.062).
num: Increasing training data size consistently improved MAE and RMSE for ARIMA and Holt-Winters, particularly for Client 1.
LSTM maintained stable performance across all training splits but showed higher complexity and data requirements that reduced practical viability.
The optimization model achieved near-zero demand gaps across all forecast scenarios while respecting capacity constraints.
num: Shared resource S2 showed slight overutilization (106%) in high-demand scenarios, flagging areas for managerial attention.
Small discrepancies in short-term forecasts were found to compound into significant cumulative cost gaps over time, reinforcing the value of dynamic short-horizon planning.
Weekly or bi-weekly use of the tool was identified as optimal for cost-effective and responsive staffing.

definitions.definition: Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average, a classical time-series model for stationary data.
Long Short-Term Memory, a recurrent neural network architecture capable of learning long-term dependencies in sequence data.
Mean Absolute Error, the average absolute forecast error.
Mean Absolute Percentage Error, a relative error metric expressed as a percentage.
Mixed-Integer Linear Programming, an optimization problem with both continuous and integer decision variables.
Root Mean Square Error, a metric that penalizes large forecast deviations.
Resource-Based Theory, a strategic management framework emphasizing optimal internal resource deployment for competitive advantage.
Predict-Then-Optimize, a two-stage framework where forecasts inform an optimization model.
Full-Time Equivalent, a measure of employee workload.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes a practical, data-driven Predict-Then-Optimize framework specifically tailored for professional service firms, addressing a gap in the literature where most forecasting-optimization systems target product-based or static planning contexts. It provides a systematic comparative evaluation of four forecasting methods (ARIMA, Holt-Winters, Prophet, LSTM) in a service-demand setting, integrating both accuracy metrics and practical deployment considerations. The work operationalizes forecast outputs through a Pyomo-based MILP model with CPLEX, demonstrating how forecast uncertainty can be incorporated via RMSE-adjusted scenarios to improve allocation robustness. Finally, it bridges predictive analytics and operational planning through an interactive Power BI dashboard, showing how advanced analytics can be made actionable for decision-makers in mid-sized firms.
directly_justifies: Prophet offers the most effective balance of forecast accuracy, interpretability, and operational usability for short-term planning in professional service firms.
Forecast bands derived from RMSE strengthen allocation model resilience and responsiveness.
Small discrepancies in short-term forecasts compound into significant cost gaps over time.
Increasing training data size improves forecast accuracy for ARIMA and Holt-Winters.
Weekly or bi-weekly tool use is optimal for cost-effective responsive staffing.
limits: Forecasting model uses only internal historical data and excludes external economic indicators that may influence demand.
Optimization model lacks input-level factors such as individual analyst skill or project complexity.
Long-range forecasting is cautioned against as rare high-impact events (e.g., COVID-19) are not modeled.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: A systematic scan across all topic domains identified relevance primarily in predictive modeling and forecasting algorithms (6.A, 6.B), as the paper's core contribution is comparing time-series forecasting methods. The optimization and allocation components map to budget/constraint optimization topics (7.A, 7.B, 7.C) and evaluation frameworks (12.A, 12.B, 12.C). Topics related to personal finance-specific domains like Filipino demographics (1.A–1.C), cultural practices (2.A–2.D), expense categorization (3.A–3.C), behavioral profiles (5.A–5.C), anomaly detection (8.A–8.C), mobile UX (9.A–9.C), privacy (10.A–10.C), engagement (11.A–11.B), savings/debt (13.A–13.C), and synthetic data (14.A) were not applicable—the paper addresses professional service workforce optimization, not personal finance. On-device vs. server inference (14.C) was considered but rejected as deployment is via Power BI with CPLEX, without explicit edge/cloud inference discussion. The paper's algorithmic comparison and optimization framing justify designation as international-algorithm-specific. Overall, the paper's topical coverage centers on forecasting evaluation and constrained optimization for operational workforce planning, with medium relevance to deployment considerations.

limitations: Analysis restricted to output-based variables (billable hours) at group level; input-level factors like individual analyst skill unavailable. [unacknowledged]
